title: Arcade vs Consensus vs Storylane Demo Suite (2026)
summary: Arcade vs Consensus compared for 2026: features, real pricing (~$42.50/seat vs $25K+/yr), best-fit use cases, and Storylane Demo Suite as a third option.
body_markdown:
Here is my thesis, stated plainly before the tables start: **Arcade vs Consensus is not one comparison, it is two different jobs wearing the same search query.** Arcade is a self-serve marketing and AI-video tool. Consensus is enterprise, sales-gated buyer enablement. Most "vs" pages quietly force you to pick a side and then sell you their own product. I run marketing at Storylane, so I have a horse in this race, but I would rather you leave this page knowing which job you actually have than clicking a demo button by accident.


I am Madhav Bhandari, CMO at Storylane. This guide does three things no top-ranking page does at once: it disambiguates the two "Arcades" you might be searching for, it gives an honest Arcade vs Consensus feature and true-cost breakdown, and it names where a third option fits. If you are here while[handling inbound demo requests](https://www.storylane.io/blog/demo-requests) and trying to pick a tool this quarter, start with the 30-second read.


> **Definition:** An *interactive demo tool* lets you capture your live product, turn it into a guided or self-guided walkthrough, and share it as a link or embed so prospects can explore the product themselves instead of waiting for a rep-led call. Arcade, Consensus, and Storylane all live in this category but attack it from opposite ends.


## Arcade vs Consensus in 30 seconds


If you only read one section, read this one. The two tools rarely compete in the same deal, because they are built for different buyers, different budgets, and different deliverables.


> **The short answer:** Choose **Arcade** if a marketer or PMM needs to publish self-serve interactive demos and AI-narrated videos fast, on a credit-card budget starting around $42.50 per seat per month. Choose **Consensus** if an enterprise sales org needs sales-gated, analytics-heavy buyer enablement wired into Salesforce, and can carry a five-figure annual contract.


Arcade skews small and mid-market, marketing-owned, and self-serve. Consensus skews enterprise, sales-owned, and procurement-heavy. The moment you frame it as "cheap tool vs expensive tool" you have already missed the real decision, which is *what deliverable your team ships and who owns it.* One buyer put the ownership question better than any analyst has:


> "I'm thinking ahead. So like is this owned by sales or is it typically owned by marketing or is it typically owned by IT? Like who typically owns this for maintenance?"
>
>
> *Chief Commercial Officer at an enterprise data management company*


That question is the whole comparison in a sentence. Hold onto it.


## Which "Arcade" and which "Consensus"? (Read this first)


This is the part no competitor page bothers to resolve, and it is the fastest way to waste an afternoon. The search results for "arcade vs consensus" are fragmented across three different products that happen to share two brand names. If you land on the wrong one, every feature and price you read is meaningless.


Here is the disambiguation, because the SERP will not do it for you. Two of the top-ten results for this query are not about demo software at all: they are about Arcade.dev, an AI-agent and MCP tooling company that gets compared with Composio. A third batch of video results points at Consensus.app, an unrelated AI research tool people pit against Perplexity. That is three different products behind two brand names, which is why the search feels so noisy.


The practical rule: check the domain before you trust a single feature or price. If the page you are reading says arcade.software and goconsensus.com, you are in the right comparison. If it says arcade.dev, merge.dev, or consensus.app, close the tab, because none of it applies to the demo-tool decision you are trying to make.

If you are comparing AI agents or MCP toolkits, you want Arcade.dev, and this page will not help you. Everyone else, the correct match-up is arcade.software versus goconsensus.com. From here on, "Arcade" means arcade.software and "Consensus" means goconsensus.com.


## What each tool actually is


Before the feature grid, a plain description of each product, because specs mean nothing without the shape of the company behind them.


**Arcade (arcade.software)** launched in 2021 as a fast, marketer-friendly way to capture a product and publish an interactive walkthrough. Its center of gravity is self-serve: sign up, record a flow, add hotspots and an AI-narrated video, and drop the demo on a landing page. It is the kind of tool a single PMM adopts without a procurement cycle, which is exactly why it spreads inside marketing teams.


**Consensus (goconsensus.com)** has been around since 2013 and sits at the opposite end. It is a Product Experience Platform built for enterprise sales and presales, where the job is to send interactive, personalized demos to buying committees and then watch what every stakeholder does with them. It assumes a sales motion, a CRM, and a deal desk. You do not casually adopt Consensus; you buy it.


Neither origin story is a flaw. They are just different animals, and the "vs" framing hides that. A marketer chasing self-serve pipeline and an enterprise AE arming a 12-person buying committee are not shopping for the same thing.

Read the table with that ownership question in mind. Arcade wins on speed-to-publish and video for[product demo and explainer videos](https://www.storylane.io/blog/saas-product-demo-and-explainer-videos) . Consensus wins on stakeholder analytics and the enterprise sales stack. Where each falls short is the interesting part, and it is the section most competitors skip.


A few rows deserve a plain-language translation, because a checkmark hides more than it reveals. Arcade's Figma import and prompt-to-video are genuinely useful for a marketer who wants a polished asset without a design queue, but its interactivity is guided rather than a true sandbox. Consensus's Demolytics and Sandbox Simulations are built for sellers who need to know which stakeholder watched what, which is a different job than publishing a demo to a landing page.


The export row is the one I would not gloss over. Arcade's MP4 and GIF output looks like portability until you realize the click-through interactivity is gone, and Consensus does not export at all, so your content is locked inside the platform. If being able to move a still-interactive demo between a website, an email, and a sales deck matters to you, weight that row heavily, because it is where both tools quietly constrain you.


## Arcade vs Consensus pricing compared (with the hidden costs)


Pricing is where "vs" pages get lazy and quote one tidy number. Do not trust a single figure from either vendor: state the billing interval, and watch the metering.


**Arcade** publishes a Free plan (one seat, roughly one published demo), then paid entry at **$42.50 per seat per month billed annually** , or about **$50 monthly** . The watch-out is the 2026 Growth-plan repricing that several observers flagged, moving to a **$297.50 per month flat structure for five seats** . That changes the math for a growing team, and Arcade layers AI credits on top, so heavy video generation meters upward.


**Consensus** is sales-gated, annual-only, with no free plan or trial. Published entry points get cited around **$600 per month for five users** (Starter) and **$1,250 per month for ten** (Pro), but real, reported contracts land closer to **$25,000 to $80,000+ per year** once you account for the enterprise features you actually bought it for. There is no swipe-your-card path in.


Here is a like-for-like, defensible way to think about first-year cost. I am comparing fully-listed annual spend, not cherry-picked headline prices.


Scenario Approx. first-year cost What drives it


Arcade, 5 seats (Growth flat) ~$3,570/yr + AI credits Flat 5-seat plan; video credits meter on usage


Consensus, entry contract ~$25,000/yr and up Annual-only, sales-quoted, enterprise features


That is roughly a 7x gap at the entry point, and it is not because one tool is a rip-off. It is because you are buying two different things. Price sensitivity is real, though, and buyers say so directly:


> "Truthfully, the lower cost is going to create less of a barrier for entry to this... so, yeah, the lower the cost, the better."
>
>
> *Product support / onboarding lead at a cybersecurity company*


The honest total-cost note: with Arcade, budget for AI-credit metering as your video volume grows; with Consensus, budget for an annual commitment before you have proven value internally, because there is no trial to de-risk it.


## Ratings & what real users say


Star ratings are a blunt instrument, so use them for segment signal, not as a verdict. The review split tells you who each tool is really serving.


On G2, Arcade sits around **4.6 out of 5 across roughly 179 reviews** , and Consensus around **4.7 out of 5 across 1,700+ reviews (per G2; verify current count at g2.com)** (G2, 2026). Both are categorized under Demo Automation, but the volumes tell the story: Consensus skews enterprise, Arcade skews SMB and mid-market.


Paraphrasing the recurring themes rather than any single review:


- **Arcade praise:** quick to learn, genuinely fast to publish, strong for marketing pages and video.
- **Arcade gripes:** interactivity gets flattened on export, and deeper enterprise controls feel thin.
- **Consensus praise:** stakeholder analytics and CRM depth that enterprise sellers love.
- **Consensus gripes:** heavier to stand up, and the interest-based demo-board approach can feel dated to teams who have used it for years.


That last point is worth sitting with. In our own conversations, a buyer who had used Consensus described its long-standing checklist and demo-board interface as losing steam. Ratings do not capture "feels dated," but deal-room conversations do.


## Who should choose Arcade, who should choose Consensus


A decision framework beats a spec sheet, so map it to your team, your motion, and your primary deliverable. These are the honest cutoffs.


**Choose Arcade if:**


- Marketing or PMM owns the demo and wants to publish without procurement.
- Your primary deliverable is a self-serve walkthrough or an AI-narrated video on a landing page.
- Budget is credit-card scale and you want a free plan to start.
- You are comparing lightweight[interactive demo tool alternatives](https://www.storylane.io/blog/tourial-alternatives) rather than an enterprise platform.


**Choose Consensus if:**


- Enterprise sales or presales owns the process and sells to buying committees.
- You need Demolytics-grade stakeholder tracking wired into Salesforce, Outreach, and Gong.
- You can carry a five-figure annual contract and have the deal volume to justify it.
- Automated, personalized demo distribution at scale is the core job.


If you read both lists and thought "half of each," you are not confused, you are the reason the two-way framing fails. Plenty of teams need marketing self-serve *and* sales depth, and neither tool is built to be both.


## What neither tool does well (and where an alternative fits)


This is the section that will rank, because no top-10 page tells you the truth about the gaps. Both tools have real limits, and they are not marketing spin.


**Export and portability.** Consensus exports nothing: your demos live inside Consensus. Arcade exports to MP4 or GIF, but that flattens the interactivity, so you lose the very thing that made the demo useful. Neither gives you a clean, portable, still-interactive asset.


**Maintenance when the UI changes.** This is the quiet tax. When your product ships new features, demos drift out of date, and someone has to re-record or re-embed. Buyers feel this pain acutely:


> "We have a self guided demo on the website and it is actually the product and we are doing some fanciness to like do a walkthrough of it. Obviously there's obvious competitive disadvantages of that that we're starting to get worried about as we roll out new features."
>
>
> *Head of GTM / tech-stack owner at an enterprise software company*


And the very practical follow-up every evaluator should ask a vendor:


> "So does the content update as and when you edit as well? Do you have to manually re embed it?"
>
>
> *Product support / onboarding lead at a cybersecurity company*


**The self-serve versus enterprise gap.** Arcade is easy but shallow at the enterprise end; Consensus is deep but heavy and marketing cannot self-serve it. If your team spans both jobs, you are stuck buying two tools or compromising on one. This is exactly where a third option earns a look. For the full landscape, see[other Consensus alternatives](https://www.storylane.io/blog/consensus-alternatives) and[how Storylane compares to other demo tools](https://www.storylane.io/blog/storylane-alternatives) .

## A quick decision scorecard


No competitor offers a structured chooser, so here is one. Answer these five and follow the tally, no visual tool required.


1. **Who owns the demo?** Marketing points toward Arcade; enterprise sales points toward Consensus; both point toward a platform that spans them.
2. **What is the primary deliverable?** A landing-page video leans Arcade; a personalized committee demo leans Consensus; a live-product interactive tour leans a sandbox-capable platform.
3. **What is the budget shape?** Credit-card and monthly favors Arcade; five-figure annual favors Consensus.
4. **How often does your UI change?** Frequent releases raise the maintenance cost of any tool, so weight ease of updates heavily.
5. **Do you need a trial to de-risk it?** If yes, Consensus is out, because there is no trial to prove value before you commit.


Count your leans. If they cluster cleanly on one tool, buy that tool. If they scatter, that scatter is the signal that you have two jobs and should evaluate a platform built to cover both.


## How Storylane Demo Suite fits (and where it does not)


Full disclosure: this is us. I am not going to pretend Storylane is the answer to every row above, so here is the honest version of where Demo Suite fits between these two.


Storylane Demo Suite is built to span the exact gap Arcade and Consensus each leave open. **Sandbox Demos** capture your live product as a fully interactive replica, so the demo behaves like the real thing rather than a flattened video. **Demo Hubs** package multiple demos into a self-serve destination a prospect can explore. The mechanism that matters: because demos are captured from the product and updated centrally, you avoid the re-record-on-every-release tax that buyers keep flagging. When your UI changes, you update once instead of manually re-embedding everywhere.


It also handles the buyer job both tools were reaching for. Prospects self-serve and self-validate before a rep call, which is exactly what buyers keep asking for:


> "We want to be able to give customers the ability to do some self validation without us having to do demos for them."
>
>
> *Director at a Sales Engineering, cybersecurity company*


On the access question the enterprise buyers raised, Demo Suite supports gating, SSO, and permissioning, so exposing demos more widely does not mean someone punching in a manual password every time. That is a real evaluation criterion, not a nice-to-have.


Where Storylane does **not** fit: if you genuinely only need a quick MP4 for a landing page and nothing more, Arcade's free plan is a lighter entry. And if you are a pure enterprise sales org that lives entirely inside a Salesforce-Outreach-Gong motion and wants a single-purpose buyer-enablement platform, Consensus's depth there is real. Demo Suite earns its place when you span both jobs, or when interactive fidelity and low maintenance matter more than a throwaway export. It is the piece that sits naturally in[your broader sales tech stack](https://www.storylane.io/blog/tools-to-build-the-best-sales-tech-stack) rather than replacing it.


One more buyer note on why "third option" is not a bait-and-switch here. Evaluators already put us on the shortlist themselves:


> "I've used a few in my past... the RFP will likely be between the three Arcade, Navattic and Storylane."
>
>
> *VP Product Marketing at an insurance / financial software company*


## How to test a demo tool before you commit


One practical habit separates teams who are happy a year later from teams who regret the contract: they prove value in their own workflow before they sign. If you cannot test a tool the way you actually work, you are buying on a sales deck, and that is exactly why Consensus's no-trial, annual-only model raises the stakes on the decision.


Favor tools that let you validate a real use case before the commitment, and treat "can I try this the way my team operates?" as a first-class question, not an afterthought. Build one demo of a genuine flow, share it with a real audience, and measure whether it lands. Buyers who get burned usually skipped that step.


Force the maintenance question early too: who keeps this current when the product changes? A tool that is cheap to buy but expensive to keep up to date is not actually cheap. The cleanest test is to build a demo, ship a product update, and watch how much manual re-work follows. That single experiment tells you more about total cost of ownership than any pricing page, and it surfaces the ownership problem before it lands on someone's plate by surprise.


**Choose Storylane Demo Suite if:**


- You need a no-code interactive demo platform your team can use on day one
- You want Demo Hubs to share multiple guided tours with prospects
- You want to test before committing: Storylane offers a free trial


## FAQ


**Which is cheaper, Arcade or Consensus?**


Arcade, by a wide margin at the entry point. Arcade starts around $42.50 per seat per month billed annually, with a free plan, while Consensus is annual-only with reported contracts commonly in the $25,000 to $80,000+ per year range. The catch is that they are priced differently because they do different jobs, so cheaper does not automatically mean better fit.


**Does Consensus have a free trial?**


No. Consensus is sales-gated and annual-only, with no free plan or self-serve trial. You go through a sales conversation and a quote, which means you cannot test it in your own workflow before committing. If a trial is important to de-risk the purchase, that alone may rule Consensus out for you.


**Is Arcade or Consensus better for enterprise?**


Consensus, if "enterprise" means selling to buying committees with deep Salesforce, Outreach, and Gong integration plus stakeholder analytics. Arcade is stronger for marketing-led, self-serve use inside SMB and mid-market teams. For teams that need both enterprise depth and marketing self-serve, neither is a clean fit, which is why a platform that spans both is worth evaluating.


**Are Arcade.software and Arcade.dev the same company?**


No, and this trips up a lot of searchers. Arcade.software is the interactive demo and AI-video tool this guide compares to Consensus. Arcade.dev is a separate company building AI-agent and MCP developer tooling, often compared with Composio. If you landed here looking for agent infrastructure, you want Arcade.dev instead.


**What is a good alternative to both Arcade and Consensus?**


If your need spans marketing self-serve and sales depth, Storylane Demo Suite is built to cover both, with interactive Sandbox Demos, Demo Hubs, and centralized updates that cut re-recording overhead. It is worth a look specifically when you would otherwise buy Arcade and Consensus for two halves of the same job.
